title: Deepening (Learning)Understanding - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton begins a three-part look at understanding, arguing that schools rarely share a clear idea of it even though many put it at the heart of their mission, and that they also over-apply it. He shows how common definitions, such as an ability to transfer concepts, collapse understanding into skill, and how linking deep understanding to factual knowledge is confusing. He notes that Wiggins and McTighe themselves warn that understanding is hard to specify and not always feasible or desirable as a goal. Pianist Andras Schiff's remark that he understands Bach a little better after twenty years becomes his anchor example: understanding is a personal meaning that emerges slowly from reflection on experience, simmering over time. He closes by distinguishing casual from professional uses of the word and why precision matters with limited school time.
points: Understanding cannot be a skill or a form of knowledge if the three categories are to be genuinely distinct.
Wiggins and McTighe's own introduction cautions that understanding is difficult to pin down and not always the right aim of teaching.
Understanding is a personal big picture that simmers up from experience, knowledge and reflection over years, as in Schiff, Dylan and the veteran Hamlet teacher.
Because school time is short, loose everyday usage of understanding wastes effort and should be tightened in professional conversation.
quotes: This can’t be right. If it’s an ability that means it’s a skill. But, and here comes the circular argument, understanding can’t be a skill because it exists as a separate entity, different from skills.

When Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe wrote that introduction to their work, they were saying something very important. Understanding is hard to grasp and it shouldn’t always be the goal. But many schools, teachers and other educators treat understanding unproblematically and proclaim it to be the overarching goal of everything they do.

Put simply, if we aren’t clear about the different goals we have for our children and students and the implications for their learning, teaching and assessment, we can very quickly become inefficient, busy, but not busy helping learning happen. With limited time and complex and important things to achieve, getting clarity is vital.
Each of these responses shares something with the others. It’s not precise and we can’t quite pin it down, but it is about a personal meaning that arises after reflective experience over time.

The point here is that we aren’t having an informal conversation where things don’t matter so much; we are having a professional one where they matter a lot. We are trying to help schools and parents do better for students by being more aware of what learning is, how it happens what it looks like, how things are learned, taught and assessed differently and what they look like at different stages and kinds of learning. Using that awareness, we want to be able to improve our students’ learning experiences.

Essentially, Understanding seems to be the personal big picture or pictures we make for ourselves of our own lives or our lives so far. Understanding is what slowly emerges when our experiences, our knowledge and abilities, our personalities and our predilections are put into the pot and allowed to simmer over time as we reflect on them. Out of all of this our understanding grows, forming the largely hidden filter for the way we approach our lives.
Some time ago, some scientists were asked when they had achieved their scientific breakthrough. Few of them gave the reply we might expect: ‘In my laboratory’.
